title: DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself
summary: Every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place to live, so a rule fixed once is fixed everywhere.
signals: the same conditional (status checks, date-window math) repeated across two handlers or controllers
a bug-fix commit that edits one of two near-identical functions but not the other
call sites that re-derive a business rule instead of asking the domain object
grep hits for the same comparison/branch across multiple entry points

roles.Order.canBeCancelled: single owner of the business rule
roles.CliCancelHandler: entry point that used to duplicate the rule
roles.ApiCancelHandler: entry point that used to duplicate the rule
roles.Clock: injected seam for testing a time-based rule without the wall clock

stages.title: Copy-pasted rule
stages.idea: The CLI and API handlers each re-implement 'can this order be cancelled?'; a fix to one copy leaves the other behind.

stages.title: One rule, two callers
stages.idea: The rule lives once on the order; both handlers call it and agree by construction.

checks: Two functions look identical today — what would tell you this is coincidental duplication rather than a DRY violation?
Why does the cancellation rule belong on the order rather than in the CLI or API handler?
What is the 'rule of three', and how does it guard against premature abstraction?
DRY is about knowledge, not text — give an example of two identical-looking blocks that should stay duplicated.
